title: platform-endpoint-sales-anchors
content:
Objective:
This is a working memo for sales and product marketing to quickly position Redwood Inference vs the big three cloud managed endpoint offers (AWS, GCP, Azure). It contains sharp win themes, likely objections, suggested rebuttals, and a short demo checklist tuned to mid-market and engineering-led buyers.

Context and audience:
- Audience: platform/product engineering managers and ML infra leads evaluating managed endpoints for production LLM features.
- Buying signals: predictable latency targets, cost overruns on public APIs, need for private VPC deployments, multi-region reliability, desire for feature parity across hosted and private deployments.

High-level takeaway (one-liner for reps):
- "For engineering teams who need predictable latency, transparent unit economics, and the ability to move from hosted to private infrastructure without rewriting code, Redwood gives the same API and rollout controls across hosted, dedicated, and private footprints — with cost and reliability levers cloud endpoints don’t expose."

Competitive snapshots (short):
- AWS (managed endpoints / Bedrock + SageMaker endpoints): super integrated into AWS infra and IAM. Strength: deep cloud ecosystem, pricing for large committed spend, and broad enterprise compliance. Weakness: opaque per-token economics on multi-vendor Bedrock models, operational variability when autoscaling, and limited first-party developer UX for inference experiments.
- GCP (Vertex AI Model Endpoints): strong MLOps tooling, nice dataset/versioning flows. Strength: easy model training->endpoint transition, integrated dataflow and monitoring. Weakness: general-purpose MLOps focus means inference optimizations (KV cache, continuous batching) are less mature; harder to get low p99 latency at scale for chat workloads.
- Azure (Azure OpenAI + Managed Inference): enterprise SLAs and identity story is strong; good for Microsoft-first shops. Weakness: limited extensibility for third-party open models, and private on-prem options are often heavier lift and vendor-locked.

Redwood win themes (packable bullets for sales):
- Production predictability: SLO-first routing, dedicated capacity options, and transparent p50/p95/p99 benchmarks by model+seq_len per customer. Reinforce: not just fast in lab — optimized for steady-state production.
- Cost clarity and levers: per-token unit economics plus prescriptive batching/quantization recommendations that we can operationalize for customers (example: 20–40% token-cost savings with prefix caching on messaging workloads). Cloud endpoints rarely provide actionable per-customer cost remediation suggestions.
- Same API, multiple footprints: customers can start on hosted for speed, then move to Dedicated or Private without code changes or rollout rewrites. This is a frequent blocker with cloud vendors where dev/test and private deployments diverge.
- Model lifecycle and rollouts: built-in canary/A-B rollouts and automatic fallback to smaller variants when capacity constrained. Cloud endpoints have some rollout features but less opinionated and less tied to inference economics.
- Developer ergonomics: first-class SDKs, examples and faststart templates oriented around production patterns (tool calling, streaming, structured output, eval hooks) — avoids ad-hoc infra glue early-stage teams otherwise need on cloud endpoints.

Direct competitive talking points (cloud-specific):
- Against AWS: "If your priority is deep AWS integration and you already accept opaque token economics and AWS billing complexity, Bedrock + SageMaker can work. If you need predictable per-request latency and clear cost remediation advice tied to payload patterns, Redwood is designed for that — with a path to private deployment without rebuilds."
- Against GCP: "Vertex is great for training/ML pipelines. But when you need low-latency chat and operationalized caching/batching, Vertex leaves more to internal engineering work. Redwood provides those inference primitives out of the box and a prescriptive ops playbook."
- Against Azure: "Azure OpenAI is an easy enterprise path for MS shops. Redwood differentiates by supporting full private deployments and a consistent API for hosted->private transitions and by providing fine-grained performance knobs and cost visibility developers actually use."

Common buyer objections and rebuttals:
- Objection: "We prefer the cloud-native path — one bill, one console."
  Rebuttal: "We integrate with cloud IAM and billing connectors; you can keep the vendor console for infra while we provide inference-level visibility and controls that the cloud console doesn't expose. Many customers run both for different needs."

- Objection: "Cloud endpoints are cheaper at our scale due to committed discounts."
  Rebuttal: "Committed discounts matter — we compete on unit economics and committed capacity contracts (Redwood Dedicated). Also, our cost recommendations frequently shrink effective usage so total spend can be materially lower even vs discounted cloud endpoints. We can model that in a short pilot."

- Objection: "Security/compliance — can’t use hosted endpoints."
  Rebuttal: "Redwood Private provides a VPC/on-prem option with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; many regulated customers pick this path to satisfy compliance without losing product parity."

Customer scenarios (quick playbook):
- Case A: AI-native startup with chat product and unpredictable growth. Start: hosted API + eval hooks. Transition: Redwood Optimize recommendations reduce token cost by 25% in month 2. Scale: move to Dedicated when throughput needs stabilize; no SDK rewrite.
- Case B: Mid-market SaaS requiring PII isolation. Start: Dedicated in customer VPC -> Full Private if needed. Use: rollout policies + tracing hooks to instrument quality regressions during model upgrades.

Demo checklist for AE/SE (30-minute flow):
1) Onboarding: show SDK quickstart and single-line generate call.
2) Cost transparency: show per-route token breakdown and sample Optimize recommendation.
3) Latency SLOs: run simple benchmark (short chat->long chat) and surface p95 differences with/without caching.
4) Rollouts: create a canary rollout, demonstrate automatic fallback.
5) Private demo: show VPC config page and KMS integration notes.

Potential risks / open questions (for product & legal follow-ups):
- Need clearer, quantifiable benchmarking artifacts that compare p99 under realistic chat loads vs each cloud vendor for 3 sequence length buckets. Action: Engineering to provide reproducible harness (JIRA RED-4210).
- Licensing/customer questions re: models in private deployments (open models vs customer-supplied models). Action: Legal & Research to draft a short FAQ.

To-dos for this doc (short list):
- Add exact cloud pricing comparison matrix for top 3 models we recommend vs vendor equivalents (attach as spreadsheet) — assigned to Eli.
- Create a 1-pager one-click slide for reps with objection bullets and the demo checklist — assigned to Simone.
- Engineering: produce benchmark harness and share raw numbers we can publish internally.

Notes to self and rep voice snippets (short soundbites):
- "Predictable inference, not just fast GPUs."
- "Move environments, not code."
- "We show you where your tokens go — and how to stop paying for what you don’t need."
